transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Linda Kenyon.
Ukrainian President Vladimir Zelensky says Ukraine will stop attacking Russian oil refineries
if Moscow suspends its attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities.
NPR's Joanna Kekissis reports Zelensky has responded to President Trump's claim that
he secured an energy truce between the two countries.
The Kremlin has not commented on the energy truce, and Zelensky says he has not been informed
about it.
In an evening video address on Sunday, he said Ukraine has proposed ways to de-escalate
the war, but Putin has only said one thing.
Yet, or no, Russia has continued to attack Ukraine since Trump announced the truce.
Trump blames Ukraine's long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries for rising fuel prices.
The strikes are Ukraine's attempt to weaken Russia's war machine.
Energy experts and even Russian authorities have said the U.S. war on Iran is primarily
driving the price hikes.
Joanna Kekissis, NPR News, cave.
Hurricane Yessus has plowed through the Florida panhandle and then north through Alabama over
the weekend.
NPR's Lauren Linnehan at WBHM says the storm left behind a path of destruction.
When Isaias made landfall on the Florida panhandle, that's where you saw those hurricane-force
winds, those 100-mile-per-hour gusts, and there were some storm surge that also led
to some, not just water damage, but then you had the winds that led to the damage of some
buildings.
But even farther inland, though Isaias weakened quickly, it did lead to some downed trees
and power outages like here where I am in Birmingham.
Unfortunately, we've learned four people lost their lives, three of them from falling trees
and one from carbon monoxide poisoning.
Coming on the heels of Isaias, that storm in the Gulf Coast now is on track for record
heat.
The Gulf Coast will have highs climbing well into the upper 80s.
Two Americans have been awarded this year's Nobel Prize in economics.
And B.R.
Scott Horsley reports.
The Nobel Committee presented the prize to economists Robert Hall of Stanford and Michael
Woodford of Columbia for their contributions to the new Keynesian understanding of how
to smooth out boom and bust cycles in the economy.
The two focused on the micro-decisions that shape broader forces of supply and demand.
Hall looked at how families make purchasing decisions, while Woodford explored the way
businesses set prices.
Both families and businesses are guided in part by expectations, so Woodford says it's
important for economic policymakers to communicate.
"Talk to people about why the things that are being done are being done."
Woodford told reporters he's surprised and elated by the award.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
Saudi Arabia has launched an investigation into how its air defenses failed to intercept
missiles and drones fired by Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
One of the attacks in Riyadh's airport killed at least 13 people.
You're listening to NPR.
Nearly 14 million homes will hit the market over the next decade, as boomers and other
older Americans sell.
But as NPR's Jennifer Ludden reports, that wave won't offer much help to first-time
buyers.
Coming years will see a 30 percent jump in housing inventory, according to a new analysis
by Realtor.com.
Most homes freed up will be larger family-sized, and that could soften the market at a time
when many people are priced out.
But only a few hundred thousand will be smaller, so-called starter homes.
In part, the report says that's because those owners are more likely to have paid off their
mortgage and stay put longer.
This generational transfer will also play out slowly.
Housing analysts say the so-called silver tsunami is not likely to close the current
housing shortage.
The oldest baby boomers turn 80 this year, a turning point when homeownership starts
to decline.
Jennifer Ludden, NPR News, Washington.
It is time for the great pumpkin.
Giant pumpkin growers are in Northern California today for the 53rd World Championship Pumpkin
Way Off in Half Moon Bay.
Four-time champion Travis Ganger from Minnesota is among the 30 pumpkin growers who have signed
up for today's event.
Despite freezing temperatures, Ganger has grown a massive pumpkin that could challenge
the world record set last week in England.
The current record is held by Ian Patton.
His giant pumpkin weighed in at 2,857 pounds.
The champion will earn $9 per pound.
I'm Linda Kenyon, NPR News in Washington.

topics.text: Zelensky says Ukraine will halt refinery strikes if Moscow suspends attacks on energy facilities
Hurricane Isaias batters Florida panhandle and Alabama, leaving four dead and widespread outages
Gulf Coast forecast to see record heat following Hurricane Isaias
Robert Hall and Michael Woodford awarded Nobel Prize in economics for boom-bust cycle research
Saudi Arabia investigates failed air defenses against Houthi missiles and drones, including Riyadh airport attack
Nearly 14 million homes expected to hit the market over next decade as older Americans sell
53rd World Championship Pumpkin Weigh-Off set for Half Moon Bay, California, with Travis Ganger competing
